transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-01 15:00 UTC
Duration: 1:18:00 (78 minutes)
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jasmine Rivera (Redwood SE), Eli Wong (Redwood), Ravi Kapoor (Orbital Tech), Maya Lin (Orbital), Carlos Duran (Orbital), Nina Park (Orbital SRE)

Summary (auto): deep technical profiling session comparing TensorRT-LLM and vLLM execution paths, kernel selection challenges, CUDA Graphs for stable throughput, KV cache behavior for multi-turn chat, quantization impact on perf/quality, and on-prem/VPC constraints for binding NVLink/GPU topology.

Topics: 
- Kernel selection heuristics (memory-bound vs compute-bound)
- TensorRT-LLM (TRT-LLM) vs vLLM tradeoffs
- CUDA Graph capture/replay warmup implications
- KV cache sizing and DRAM/GPU residency policies
- Batching strategies and tail-latency vs cost tradeoffs
- Quantization profiles and end-to-end accuracy regressions
- VPC/on-prem networking, HBM vs host memory fallback

[00:00] Samir: okay everyone hi thanks for joining, um quick intros. I'm Samir, AE at Redwood, jasmine and eli from engineering will do most of the profiling talk.
[00:18] Ravi: hey thanks, ravi here, head of platform at Orbital. excited — we want to validate perf before greenlighting a Dedicated cluster.
[00:28] Jasmine: great, scope for today is kernel selection notes, real traces, and then walk through CUDA graphs and how that affects cold-starts. we'll surface what we saw on p3/p4 like hardware and on A100 vs h100.
[00:45] Maya: small ask - we run mixed workloads, some short completions and 2k token chat tails, and we care about 95th percentile latency under 200ms for short prompts.
[00:58] Eli: noted, we'll map that to batching policies and KV cache hit rates.

[01:10] [Jasmine screen share of perf sheet] 
[01:22] Jasmine: first slide, kernel selection: the runtime picks different matmul kernels depending on sequence length, hidden size and dtype. for fp16 on H100 we saw faster kernels for seq <= 512, but beyond that the tiling changes and memory-bound kernels kick in. sometimes the selector chooses a 'safe' kernel that allocates more temp memory, that's a big source of perf cliffs.
[01:52] Carlos: is that auto-selected by cuBLAS/cuDNN or by the serving runtime?
[01:58] Jasmine: it's a mix — the runtime has a kernel-cost model, it will prefer cuBLAS batchedGemm paths for certain shapes, but for a few ops we fallback to TRT-LLM custom kernels that fuse attention + rotary, etc. small mis-specs in shape inference can flip the path.

[02:20] [00:02:20] Ravi: we've seen occasional 2-3x slowdowns during bursty tail requests, sounds like this could be it.
[02:29] Samir: yes those cliff events often align with sequence-length transitions or when KV cache spills to host memory.

[02:38] Jasmine: kv cache — important note: vLLM keeps KV cache resident in GPU memory per session by default, which gives lowest latency for multi-turn but uses a lot of HBM. TensorRT-LLM variants often implement a compressed KV format and can stream cold KV pages to host memory or NVMe. the tradeoff is latency vs memory cost.
[03:10] Nina: for our on-prem racks we have 80GB HBM on H100, but some jobs are multi-session so we can't keep all KV resident. do you support partial resident + eviction?
[03:22] Eli: yes, Redwood runtime supports LRU eviction and we can archive cold KV to host DDR; but crossing PCIe has a big penalty. our recommendation for tight SLOs is to pin hot sessions on dedicated GPUs or use a bigger HBM instance.

[03:45] [03:45] Jasmine: moving to CUDA Graphs — capturing a graph for the common token generation path reduces CPU/GPU synchronization overhead. however, graphs are brittle: if sequence length or attention mask shape changes, the graph can't be reused and runtime falls back to immediate mode, which increases latency.
[04:10] Maya: so for chat where length grows over time, graphs may not help?
[04:18] Jasmine: you can capture graphs for a set of bucketed lengths — e.g., 64, 128, 256, 512 — and replay the nearest. that reduces graph misses but increases memory for precompiled graphs. also, warmup is key: first few tokens still pay compilation cost.

[04:40] [04:40] Ravi: what about warm start vs cold start numbers?
[04:45] Eli: we measured cold-start token latency on H100 for a 2k model: first token ~320ms cold, down to ~18ms steady-state with CUDA graphs and KV resident. vLLM steady-state was ~22ms with aggressive batching. numbers vary by batch size.

[05:10] Jasmine: these numbers reflect our bench harness where we keep per-session batch=1. batching increases throughput but hurts tail latency; so we typically use dynamic batching with SLO-aware thresholds.
[05:28] Carlos: curious on TRT-LLM vs vLLM — in our experiments TRT had lower average latency but vLLM showed better handling of mem fragmentation?
[05:37] Jasmine: yup that's common. TRT-LLM can aggressively fuse kernels and use TensorCores for big speedups, but its memory allocator and fused op graph sometimes require contiguous buffers which shows fragmentation. vLLM's allocator is more flexible but less fused; it benefits from custom allocator heuristics.

[06:00] [06:00] Maya: any notes about quantization? we want to try 4-bit.
[06:07] Eli: quantization (4-bit GPTQ/QLoRA-style) gives big memory wins and often a 1.5-2x throughput boost, but you must watch accuracy regressions. we run targeted evals on your prompt set and include a quality budget — e.g., accept up to 2% F1/ROUGE drop. some kernels for 4-bit aren't as optimized in TRT-LLM yet.
[06:35] Samir: also mixed precision fp16 + 4-bit hybrid schemes are helpful: keep attention in fp16 and weights in 4-bit. reduces quant noise on sensitive ops.

[06:50] [06:50] Jasmine: network/VPC notes: when running in VPC or on-prem, NVLink topology and multi-GPU peer access matter for KV sharing across workers. if NVLink isn't present you pay serialization costs. Redwood's private deployment supports colocated pods with GPU affinity to preserve NVLink channels.
[07:15] Nina: our rack uses Mellanox IB, but we'd need guidance on MTU and RDMA setup for low-latency KV streaming.
[07:24] Eli: we'll share config best-practices — Jumbo frames, tuned numactl, and pinned interrupts.

[07:38] [07:38] Jasmine shares pprof flamegraphs
[07:45] Jasmine: flamegraph shows two hotspots: matmul kernel and attention softmax kernel. attention softmax becomes memory-bound at long context lengths because of repeated reductions and softmax ops. fuseable softmax implementations in TRT sometimes reduce DRAM traffic.
[08:10] Ravi: are there quick knobs to tune to avoid the slow kernel path?
[08:16] Jasmine: yes: tune your sequence bucketing, force a different kernel using runtime flags, or adjust tile sizes in the kernel registry. Redwood's runtime exposes a 'kernel_override' flag for experimenting, but we recommend tests before production.

[08:40] [08:40] Maya: we run multi-tenant; what's recommended for isolation — dedicated vs shared?
[08:48] Samir: Dedicated GPU pools give predictable HBM for KV and consistent kernel selection because shapes are stable. Shared hosting with clever scheduling and caching works too if you accept more variability and use QoS shaping.

[09:05] Jasmine: demo time — i'll play two short traces. Trace A: TRT-LLM, H100, 8k context, partial quant, shows throughput 2.1 tokens/ms and p95 ~45ms after warm. Trace B: vLLM, H100, 8k context, full fp16, shows 1.6 tokens/ms but p95 ~30ms in small prompt cases because of less batching.
[09:40] [09:40] audio hiccup - partial drop
[09:47] Ravi: you said TRT had higher throughput but worse p95 sometimes?
[09:51] Jasmine: correct — that was for large batch throughput. For single-session latency, TRT fused kernels may win on average but degrade at certain sequence transitions. vLLM's approach keeps tail latency more stable.

[10:12] [10:12] Nina: curious re: CUDA Graphs and dynamic shapes — if we bucket lengths, how many buckets do you find sweet spot?
[10:20] Eli: typically 4-6 buckets covering short/med/long/very-long; depends on distribution. more buckets reduce misses but cost more memory and compile time.

[10:40] Jasmine: Q: kernel selection for attention: sometimes we observed the runtime choosing a TF32-like kernel on H100 when fp16 would be better due to a heuristic bug; we filed an internal bug and can force override. small details like epsilon in softmax reduction change the numerical path and kernel pick.

[11:05] [11:05] Carlos: do you have automation to detect kernel cliff events in prod?
[11:11] Eli: yes we collect per-op latencies and expose alerts when an op latency jumps by >30% relative to baseline; we also surface kernel ids so engineer can correlate to a kernel change.

[11:30] [11:30] Maya: about measuring accuracy regression for quant: what's your process?
[11:35] Jasmine: we run a two-tier eval: unit prompt-level checks (per-prompt similarity, logprob drift) and downstream tests (QA F1, ranking metrics). we ship a report with delta distributions.

[12:00] [12:00] Ravi: network perf for on-prem — if we do dedicated, what's the recommended NVLink topology?
[12:06] Eli: full-mesh NVLink inside the enclosure when possible; for multi-node, RDMA + NVMe offload for cold KV pages. we have a template for Dell/Lenovo racks we can share.

[12:28] [12:28] Jasmine: we should talk about cost math: quantization and compressed KV reduce HBM requirements enabling smaller instance types and lower unit cost. CUDA graphs reduce CPU overhead so you can run more workers per host. but engineering cost to implement bucketization and eviction policies exists.

[12:52] [12:52] Samir: ok let's surface the POC plan — run a 3-day POC: day 1 run TRT-LLM baseline, day 2 run vLLM baseline, day 3 run quant+CUDA-graphs + eviction policy. we'll measure p50/p95/p99, token throughput, and quality metrics.

[13:18] [13:18] Maya: sounds good. one more Q: can Redwood's private deployment integrate with our KMS/HSM for key management?
[13:26] Samir: yes, we support external KMS integrations and can run in air-gapped mode with customer-managed keys.

[13:40] [13:40] wrap-up recap by Samir
[13:46] Samir: recap: we'll share benchmarks, config best-practices, and schedule the POC. Jasmine/Eli will send the kernel override checklist and graph warmup scripts. Maya will upload prompt set.

[13:58] Ravi: thanks all, appreciate the depth.
[14:05] Carlos: thanks.
